Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

The two things to compare are proposals, not things already installed. Proposal A is a continuous teal floor stripe from both entrances, branching to each bay group and to the ticket desk, toilets and lifts. It also has overhead blade signs with bay numbers and destination names, a larger route map at each entrance, and smaller printed maps at the lift and ticket desk. The stripe is proposed as adhesive vinyl. The station manager says floor cleaning is done every night and that replacement vinyl is normally ordered in batches, rather than one small piece at a time.

Proposal B has no continuous floor line. It puts two large digital information kiosks in the concourse, one near each entrance, and freestanding printed maps at both entrances and beside the lift. It keeps the overhead bay-number signs but adds destination names beneath the numbers. A smaller screen would sit near the ticket desk. The kiosk design has a text search, a list of departures, and a route diagram; the designer says the screen can be updated when a bay changes. The proposal assumes staff can update it, but there is no supplied figure for staffing time or update costs. Printed maps would also be revised when the layout changes. The station manager says the concourse has power outlets by both entrances, but there is no information about network reliability or screen repair arrangements. Please don't fill those gaps with guesses.

Compare both proposals against the criteria I have supplied, not just which one sounds modern. The first criterion is route-finding: could a first-time passenger get from either entrance to the correct bay, ticket desk, toilets, or lift, including if they need to transfer between the frequent bays 1 to 6 and a coach at bays 7 to 12? Consider that overhead signs are already there and that the only current route map is by the ticket desk. The second is visibility and wayfinding under real conditions. Please give a balanced comparison, with the criteria easy to find and the evidence for each option kept distinct from claims made by a designer. I am not asking you to pick a winner or to invent a score. Keep the conclusion limited to what the supplied information supports, and clearly label unknowns. Use only the information below, distinguish stated facts from claims, and clearly identify missing information as unknown rather than guessing.

## Station context

North Quay Bus Exchange is a municipal station in a coastal town. It has twelve bus bays and an indoor concourse. Harbour Road is the east entrance; Market Lane is the west entrance. The ticket desk is just inside the east entrance. The toilets and one lift are near the middle of the concourse. Stairs and another lift lead to the pedestrian bridge at the west end. Currently, the only route map is beside the ticket desk, and bay numbers appear on overhead signs. Engine noise can make spoken announcements difficult to hear. During peak periods, buses at bays 1–6 usually arrive every four to seven minutes; bays 7–12 serve less frequent coach services. On Saturdays, the produce market crowds the pavement outside Market Lane, but that entrance remains open.

## Proposals to compare

**Proposal A:** A continuous teal floor stripe would run from both entrances and branch toward each bay group, the ticket desk, toilets, and lifts. Overhead blade signs would show bay numbers and destination names. Larger route maps would be placed at both entrances, with smaller printed maps by the lift and ticket desk. Where the stripe crosses boarding lanes, it would stop and matching arrows would appear on the wall on either side. The designer claims that people can follow a color route without stopping to read much; assess this claim against the supplied details rather than treating it as a proven result. The stripe would be adhesive vinyl. The station manager says floors are cleaned nightly and replacement vinyl is normally ordered in batches, not as individual small pieces.

**Proposal B:** There would be no continuous floor line. Two large digital information kiosks would be placed in the concourse, one near each entrance, with freestanding printed maps at both entrances and beside the lift. Existing overhead bay-number signs would remain, with destination names added beneath the numbers. A smaller screen would be placed near the ticket desk. The kiosks would have text search, departure lists, and a route diagram. The designer says the screen could be updated when a bay changes. The proposal assumes staff can update it, but no staffing-time or update-cost figures are supplied. Printed maps would also need revision when the layout changes. The station manager says power outlets are available by both entrances; network reliability and screen-repair arrangements are not specified.

## Comparison criteria

1. **Route-finding:** Consider whether a first-time passenger could get from either entrance to the correct bay, ticket desk, toilets, or lift, including when transferring between frequent services at bays 1–6 and a coach at bays 7–12. Account for the existing overhead signs and the current location of the only route map.
2. **Visibility and wayfinding in real conditions:** Consider the engine noise, the Saturday market crowd outside Market Lane, and the fact that passengers may enter from either side. Do not assume all passengers see or hear information in the same way.
3. **Accessibility:** Address mobility access, low vision, and passengers who may not read English well, using only the features actually specified. Neither proposal has specified tactile guidance, audio features, languages, or screen-reader support; do not attribute these features to either option.
4. **Installation and disruption:** Compare the stated work: laying vinyl and fitting signs or maps for Proposal A, and fitting kiosks and screens for Proposal B. Closure dates, contractor plans, and disruption estimates have not been supplied; identify these as unknown rather than estimating them.
5. **Upkeep and operational fit:** For Proposal A, consider nightly cleaning and batch ordering of replacement vinyl. For Proposal B, consider map revisions, staff updates, power outlets, and the missing information about network reliability and screen repairs.
6. **Information consistency:** Consider whether information would stay consistent across signs, maps, and screens, based only on the supplied proposal details. Do not invent an update workflow.

last thursday evening i went to the cedar bench workshop, a small woodworking makerspace in the old freight depot on mason street. i was there for their monthly member meeting, which started at six thirty in the room behind the tool library. rain was tapping on the high windows, and people kept leaving wet jackets on the backs of chairs. there were eleven of us by the time mara, the coordinator, began. a long maple board was being used as the meeting table, with a coffee ring near one end and a row of pencil marks that nobody seemed to mind.

mara started with the usual shop update, but she had put a few things on paper because, as she said, “we keep having the same conversation and then forgetting which part we agreed to talk about.” the dust collector was running loudly again, mostly when the wide-belt sander was on. tom had checked the outside vent and found a strip of loose mesh, but he had not opened the motor housing. mara said she was not asking anyone to fix it during the meeting, only to decide who could look at it with her on saturday. dev volunteered, as long as they first checked the manual, since he had never worked on that model.

the next discussion was about the beginner bench area. two new members had tried to use it on monday and found the clamps mixed in with the hand planes. the room itself is narrow, so there was disagreement about whether a second rack would make things easier or leave too little walking space. jo thought a wall rack could work if it sat beside the sharpening station, while leah said that spot was already awkward when people carried long boards through. nobody measured the space at the meeting. instead, they agreed to take a tape measure and a piece of cardboard over there before ordering anything. that was a proposal, not a purchase decision, mara pointed out.

1. items people wanted to keep in view

- the cabinet key stays on the hook by the sign-in clipboard, rather than in the drawer where it had been found twice.
- the maple offcuts are for member projects, but anything shorter than six inches should go in the kindling bin unless someone labels it for a specific use.
- safety glasses are still required at the lathe, even for a quick test cut. mara repeated that because one person had asked whether the rule was different for turning soft wood.
- the small bandsaw has a new blade, but its fence has not been checked for square yet. nobody was asked to use it before that check.

we spent a while on the offcut rule because the bin label had disappeared. ben said that short pieces were useful for testing stain colors, and he had kept a shoebox of them under the finishing bench. mara said that was fine for labeled pieces, but the box could not become another unmarked pile. they did not decide on a new label design. someone suggested a yellow card, and leah wrote it on the back of the meeting sheet so it would not get lost before the next discussion.

after that, mara raised the saturday open-house table. the neighborhood association had asked whether the shop could bring a small display to its spring repair fair in april. the request was for examples of simple repairs, not for anyone to promise free work at the event. tom thought the shop could show a chair with a repaired rung and a drawer with a replaced runner. jo had a small stool that might be suitable, although she wanted to check whether its glue-up would be finished by then. the group did not commit to attending. mara said she would reply that the makerspace was considering it and ask how much table space was available.

there was also a brief conversation about the ventilation sign near the finishing corner. the sign says to keep the door closed while oil-based finishes are in use, but people sometimes prop it open when carrying in lumber. dev said he had noticed it wedged with a scrap of pine last week. leah said the door was heavy and the closer was slow, so a sign alone might not solve the problem. no one suggested changing the ventilation setup. they talked instead about putting a small doorstop in the office and taking it out only when lumber was being moved. mara was unsure whether that would be more confusing, and asked everyone to leave it as it was until they could discuss it with the building manager.

Instead, they agreed to take a tape measure and a piece of cardboard over there before ordering anything. Mara pointed out that this was a proposal, not a purchase decision.

1. Items people wanted to keep in view

- The cabinet key stays on the hook by the sign-in clipboard, rather than in the drawer where it had been found twice.
- The maple offcuts are for member projects, but anything shorter than six inches should go in the kindling bin unless someone labels it for a specific use.
- Safety glasses are still required at the lathe, even for a quick test cut. Mara repeated this because one person had asked whether the rule was different for turning soft wood.

Mara said she would reply that the makerspace was considering it and ask how much table space was available.

There was also a brief conversation about the ventilation sign near the finishing corner. It says to keep the door closed while oil-based finishes are in use, but people sometimes prop it open when carrying in lumber. Dev said he had noticed it wedged with a scrap of pine last week. Leah said the door was heavy and the closer was slow, so a sign alone might not solve the problem. No one suggested changing the ventilation setup. Instead, they discussed putting a small doorstop in the office and taking it out only when lumber was being moved. Mara was unsure whether that would be more confusing and asked everyone to leave things as they were until they could discuss it with the building manager.

He wrote “second coat?” on masking tape and stuck it beside the sample rather than deciding right then whether it needed another coat. The sander was off by then, and the dust collector sounded quieter, though nobody had checked the motor. Outside, the rain had stopped. I left with the cardboard rack template still on the table and the yellow-card suggestion written on the meeting sheet."}]

I'm going through each polish item one by one, checking whether the edits stay faithful to meaning. The first one looks fine as a clean simplification, but the second swaps "people" for "members" which subtly adds an assumption not in the original, and shifts a causal "because" into a softer "while."

For the Portuguese item, I'm comparing each clause: "era pequena" and "soaram" work as valid rephrasings, the subjunctive correction is right, but "Gostei de a regente ter explicado" shifts from liking how she explained to liking that she explained, a small meaning change. The swap from "fez eu acompanhar" to "me ajudou a acompanhá-la" also softens the causation slightly but adds the object "a peça," which seems acceptable.

Moving to prompt-0029, it's a longer item starting with a stray "lowercase" word that might be a dictation artifact or leaked instruction. Checking for dropped conditions, I notice the output about engine noise omits the original detail "when buses are pulling in," and I'm now checking whether the toilets/lift location detail survived the rewrite.

I also spot that "compare both proposals against the criteria... not just which one sounds modern" lost its qualifier, and more importantly, the instruction to keep the comparison useful for a station team that has to discuss it got dropped entirely — that's a loss of supplied audience context, not just stylistic noise.

Moving to polish-0016, the storage-room chairs rewrite and the "anyone who needs" phrasing both hold up fine — that one passes. For polish-0021, "we did the walk through blocks" becoming "we walked through the blocks" also reads fine so far.

Checking polish-0018, the open-seating to "first-come, first-served" rewrite is a slight stretch but roughly equivalent, and the rest of the changes (conductor phrasing, "visitors may watch," doors open, paragraph breaks) all seem acceptable, so that one passes too. Now I'm starting to review polish-0009, which is longer, beginning with the "monthly member meeting" phrase.

The Saturday open-house table versus the April repair fair seems like a minor contradiction worth noting, but otherwise this all checks out fine.

I'm going through each polish item one by one, checking whether the edits stay faithful to meaning. The first one looks fine as a clean simplification, but the second swaps "people" for "members" which subtly adds an assumption not in the original, and shifts a causal "because" into a softer "while."

For the Portuguese item, I'm comparing each clause: "era pequena" and "soaram" work as valid rephrasings, the subjunctive correction is right, but "Gostei de a regente ter explicado" shifts from liking how she explained to liking that she explained, a small meaning change. The swap from "fez eu acompanhar" to "me ajudou a acompanhá-la" also softens the causation slightly but adds the object "a peça," which seems acceptable.

Moving to prompt-0029, it's a longer item starting with a stray "lowercase" word that might be a dictation artifact or leaked instruction. Checking for dropped conditions, I notice the output about engine noise omits the original detail "when buses are pulling in," and I'm now checking whether the toilets/lift location detail survived the rewrite.

I also spot that "compare both proposals against the criteria... not just which one sounds modern" lost its qualifier, and more importantly, the instruction to keep the comparison useful for a station team that has to discuss it got dropped entirely — that's a loss of supplied audience context, not just stylistic noise.

Moving to polish-0016, the storage-room chairs rewrite and the "anyone who needs" phrasing both hold up fine — that one passes. For polish-0021, "we did the walk through blocks" becoming "we walked through the blocks" also reads fine so far.

Checking polish-0018, the open-seating to "first-come, first-served" rewrite is a slight stretch but roughly equivalent, and the rest of the changes (conductor phrasing, "visitors may watch," doors open, paragraph breaks) all seem acceptable, so that one passes too. Now I'm starting to review polish-0009, which is longer, beginning with the "monthly member meeting" phrase.

The Saturday open-house table versus the April repair fair seems like a minor contradiction worth noting, but otherwise this all checks out fine.
